questions.title: Objects practice 1
questions.prompt: Which uses the value in key?
choices: student[key]
student.key
student->key
student(key)
questions.explanation: Brackets evaluate the variable, while dot notation searches for a property literally named key.

questions.title: Objects practice 2
choices: the object is copied
a const error
questions.explanation: Both variables refer to one object, so the property change is visible through first.

questions.title: Trace Objects
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: Dot notation reads a fixed name, while brackets use the string stored in field. The resulting output is 'Ada\nCS'.

questions.title: Objects practice 5
questions.prompt: Given `const key = "credits";`, why use `student[key]` instead of `student.key`?
choices: Brackets use the variable's value, so it reads student.credits
Dot and bracket access are identical here
student.key reads the credits property too
Brackets only work on arrays, not objects
questions.explanation: `student[key]` evaluates `key` to the string "credits" and reads that property, giving `student.credits`. `student.key` looks for a property literally named "key", which does not exist, so it returns undefined. Bracket access works on objects and is exactly how you use a computed property name.

questions.title: Missing properties
questions.prompt: What happens when JavaScript reads an object property that does not exist?
choices: It returns `undefined`, which can cause trouble later if the code treats it like a real value.
It creates the missing property automatically.
It searches every other object for the property.
It throws immediately for every missing property read.
questions.explanation: A missing property read usually gives `undefined`. The danger often appears on the next line, when code tries to call a method or read a nested property from that missing value. Optional fields should be checked before use.

questions.title: Dot notation
questions.prompt: When is dot notation the clearest way to read an object property?
choices: Mutate a shared object when an independent copy is needed.
Use dots for fixed keys.
Store unrelated data under one large object.
Assume assigning an object creates a deep copy.
questions.explanation: Dot notation is clear when the property name is fixed in the code, such as `student.name`. It tells the reader exactly which property is being used. Brackets are better when the key comes from a variable or expression.

questions.title: Computed keys
questions.prompt: A property name is stored in a variable called `field`. Which access style matches that situation?
choices: Ignore optional properties before using nested values.
Use arrays when named properties would be clearer.
Use brackets for computed keys.
Overwrite a property instead of updating the intended one.
questions.explanation: Bracket notation evaluates the expression inside the brackets, so `student[field]` uses the key stored in `field`. Dot notation would look for a literal property named `field`, which is a different question.

questions.title: Optional properties
questions.prompt: A profile object may or may not include `middleName`. What should the code do before using it?
choices: Compare objects by their printed JSON text.
Depend on property order for program meaning.
Use a property before checking it exists.
Check optional properties.
questions.explanation: Optional properties need an existence check, fallback, or optional chaining before later code relies on them. That keeps normal missing data from turning into confusing `undefined` behavior somewhere else.

questions.title: Independent mutation
questions.prompt: Two variables should be able to change independently. What should happen before mutating one object?
choices: Copy before independent mutation.
Copy only the top level when nested data also needs independence.
Use dynamic keys without validating their names.
Put methods and data together without a clear relationship.
questions.explanation: Object assignment copies the reference, not a separate object. If two variables need independent state, make the appropriate copy before mutation. Nested objects may need deeper copying depending on what will change.

questions.title: Named properties
questions.prompt: Why group related values into an object?
choices: Use one object to represent several different shapes at once.
Group related values under named properties.
Forget that objects are passed by reference.
Treat undefined as the same as every valid value.
questions.explanation: An object gives related values names, which makes code easier to read than relying on positions alone. It is a good fit when the data describes one thing with several properties.
